title: "I will not rise"
hookLine: he resolves not to move until he awakens
last: ASSATTHA — A SEAT IS A DECISION.

cards: A workout you'll quit if it gets too hard. A writing session with the phone face-up beside you. Ten minutes of meditation, and at minute four a voice says, you know, that's probably enough.
An exit built into everything can feel safe. It also means never finding out what's on the other side of staying. The wanderer is sitting on his seat of grass under the great fig tree, facing east.
The sun is going down. And before the night begins, he makes a vow.

teach.h: I WILL NOT RISE FROM THIS SEAT.
teach.b: The later telling gives the vow in dramatic words. Let my skin and sinews and bones dry up. Let the flesh and blood in my body wither.
But I will not rise from this seat until I have found complete awakening. It sounds like the old austerities, but it isn't. He's not starving now; he's eaten.
He's not forcing his breath. He's just decided not to leave.
That difference, forcing or staying, is the whole lesson of the last two weeks.

The Pali canon has a similar resolve in the Buddha's own words: let only skin and sinews and bones remain, but my effort will not slacken until I reach what can be reached. And what he's staying for has a name: bodhi.

teach.h: BODHI — FROM BUDH, TO WAKE UP.
teach.b: It means awakening, from a root, budh, that means to wake up, to become aware, to understand. The same root is in the word Buddha, which comes soon.
In Buddhist teaching, bodhi is not a trance, or a vision, or a feeling of bliss. It's pictured as waking up, the way you wake from a dream and see the room as it actually is.
That's why the tree became the Bodhi tree, and the place Bodh Gaya.
Staying put, in Buddhist practice, doesn't mean gritting your teeth through pain. It means not running.
When restlessness says get up, you notice it, and stay. When boredom says check your phone, you notice it, and stay. The noticing is the practice.

how: Some Buddhist meditators begin a sit or a retreat by making a quiet resolve (adhitthana) to stay for a set time, and resolve is counted among the perfections in Theravada teaching.

o: a deep trance beyond all thought
a vision of light seen in meditation
awakening, like waking up from a dream

games.q: what's inside the vow — tap the pairs.
p: I will not rise from this seat

s: the vow under the tree was another starvation practice
he had eaten. this wasn't forcing; it was deciding not to leave.
bodhi and Buddha come from the same root
budh: to wake up, to become aware.
bodhi means a trance or a vision
it means awakening, like waking from a dream and seeing the room as it is.

games.q: you sit under the tree as the sun goes down. before the night begins, what do you decide?
o: to try for an hour, then rest.
not to rise from this seat until you awaken.
to wait and see how the night goes.
games.why: he vows not to rise until he awakens: let skin and sinews and bones dry up, but he will not leave the seat.

practice: Make a small vow, the size of today: for these two minutes, I'll stay, not perfectly still, not perfectly calm, just here.
When the mind says that's enough, notice it and stay; when an itch comes, see if it passes; when a thought pulls you away, come back to the breath. You're not fighting anything, just not leaving.

wordCard.voice: Bodhi. Awakening, from the root budh, to wake up. What the wanderer vowed not to rise without, and the name of the tree he sat beneath.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: awakening, from the root budh, to wake up, to know.

carryVoice: Your line: stay put. The night under the tree is just beginning. See you there tomorrow.
